headline: Healey presses utilities to return $1.5 billion to New England ratepayers
dek: The Massachusetts governor wants Eversource, National Grid and Unitil to disclose customers’ shares and issue transmission refunds before the federal May 2027 deadline.
body: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey is pressing three utilities serving the state to begin returning customers’ share of an estimated $1.5 billion refund owed to electricity customers across New England. In a letter sent Tuesday, Healey urged Eversource, National Grid and Unitil to stop waiting for the federal deadline and work with ISO New England and other transmission owners on an earlier payment plan. The [governor’s announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-calls-on-transmission-utilities-to-immediately-refund-15-billion-owed-to-customers) did not give a Massachusetts-specific dollar amount or a date when individual bills will be credited.

The money comes from a dispute over the return on equity, or profit rate, that transmission companies were allowed to collect through regional electric rates. Those charges support the high-voltage network that moves power into and around the six-state New England grid. They are separate from the price of electricity itself and from the local distribution charges on a household’s bill, so the eventual refund may not appear as a simple across-the-board check or identical credit for every customer.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s March 19, 2026 Opinion 594 found that New England transmission owners had collected an unreasonably high return for years and ordered refunds for the difference between the higher rate and the lawful rate set in the decision. The [ISO-NE participant report](https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/100035/npc-2026-05-07-composite4.pdf) describes the refund obligation as covering the gap between the higher return collected and the lawful return established by FERC. The proceeding covers a long period of transmission billing rather than a single recent rate case.

FERC first directed the owners to complete the refunds within 30 days. After the utilities and ISO New England asked for more time, the commission extended the payment deadline to May 20, 2027, with a refund report due June 4, 2027, according to the [ISO-NE participant report](https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/100035/npc-2026-05-07-composite4.pdf). Healey’s complaint is that customers should not have to wait through another winter for money that regulators have already determined must be returned.

The governor asked Eversource, National Grid and Unitil to provide Massachusetts-specific answers by Oct. 27. Her requests include a clear accounting of how much is owed to the state’s customers, a schedule for returning it and an explanation of how the money will reach households and businesses. Those details matter because transmission owners serve customers across state lines and the refund obligation is being calculated through regional billing arrangements.

Independent reporting by [NBC Boston](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/healey-pressures-utilities-to-issue-refunds-before-winter-bills-hit/4030467/) said the companies are not legally required to make the payments until late spring and that Healey’s letter went to utility executives and the head of ISO New England. The report also described the refunds as tied to transmission rates that included an excessive return on equity for more than a decade. That timing distinction is important: the governor is demanding an accelerated voluntary process, not announcing that credits have already been approved for the next monthly bill.

The dispute reaches beyond Massachusetts. ISO-NE’s materials identify transmission owners and affected parties in Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont, including Eversource, National Grid, Unitil, Rhode Island Energy and Vermont transmission companies. The regional scope means a Massachusetts customer’s eventual amount will depend on the company serving that customer, historic usage and the final accounting approved through the federal process. Neither the governor’s release nor the federal materials provide a reliable per-household estimate.

There is also a separate fight over future earnings. Healey and Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell have opposed a transmission-owner proposal to raise the base return on equity from 9.57% to 11.39%, according to the governor’s office. The proposed increase is not the refund itself, but it helps explain why the administration is treating the schedule and size of the repayment as part of a broader energy-affordability debate while winter bills are approaching.

For now, the next concrete step is the Oct. 27 response deadline set by Healey, followed by the utilities’ accounting and payment plan. Customers should not assume that the $1.5 billion estimate represents a guaranteed check or that they need to file a new application; the public announcement does not yet say how credits will be distributed. The central unresolved questions are how much Massachusetts customers are owed, whether utilities agree to move payments forward and how the regional refund will be reflected on future bills.
location: Massachusetts and the New England power grid
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Healey presses utilities on $1.5 billion New England refunds
seoDescription: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey wants utilities to explain and accelerate refunds tied to excessive transmission profits owed to New England ratepayers.
